paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.32 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 10 (Part 9)
paragraphs.text: In a proceeding under the Class Proceedings Act or in a representative action, the Court, in determining whether a costs award should be made against the unsuccessful representative party, may take into account one or more of the following factors, in addition to any other factors the Court considers appropriate: (a) the public interest; (b) whether the action involved a novel point of law; (c) whether the proceeding or action was a test case; (d) access to justice considerations.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.32:1 Rule 10.32 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.32. In Andriuk v. Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2014 ABQB 28, 2014 CarswellAlta 61, 578 A.R. 85, 60 C.P.C. (7th) 437, Madam Justice Martin discussed the approach to follow when considering an award of costs in class proceedings. She said, at paragraphs 1, 3, and 4: 1 S.L. MARTIN J.:—This judgment concerns one issue: should the court exercise its discretion to award a multiplier on the costs the plaintiffs agreed to pay after their application to have their claim certified as a class action was dismissed. Alberta is one of a few jurisdictions in Canada that permits costs awards in class proceedings. Nevertheless, any award remains in the discretion of the court, in accordance with the Rules of Court. It is possible that costs will not always follow the event when an application for certification is dismissed because of the underlying goals of class proceedings: the aggregation of claims to pursue efficiency, access to justice and behaviour modification. … 3 Courts have the discretion to award enhanced costs. According to Morrison Petroleum Ltd. v. Phoenix Canada Ltd. (1998), 236 AR 95 some relevant factors to consider when addressing claimed increases to the tariffs include: the difficulty and complexity of the issues; the importance of the case between the parties and or the community at large; the length of the trial; the position and relationship of the parties and their conduct prior to and during the course of the trial; and other factors which may affect the fairness of a cost award. Such factors may have some bearing in a class proceeding. See also Eaton v. HMS Financial Inc., 2010 ABQB 364. 4 The defendants claim that a multiplier is justified based on the difficult and complex issues in this case, the conduct of the litigation, and the resulting length of the application. It is to be remembered that an application for certification as a class action is a preliminary and interlocutory step governed by legislation. If certification is denied, the action proceeds as an individual action, based upon the filed statement of claim. The certification process adds another step in the litigation and involves a multi-part statutory test. To some extent, the mere framework of class proceedings adds difficulty and complexity to any litigation. However, in my view it is not appropriate to conclude that enhanced costs should apply automatically to certification proceedings. The factor of the difficulty and complexity of the issues ought to be gauged by reference to other certification applications. In the end, Madam Justice Martin concluded that in the case before her: 6 However, based on the other factors I have concluded that no multiplier is justified in the circumstances. The complexity and delay are dealt with by allowing recovery for each step in fact taken and the missing elements led to the dismissal of the application. This matter is of significance to the plaintiffs and the larger investor community. Each party has argued the misconduct of the other and case law supports the use of multipliers to discourage behaviours that increase the duration and expense of litigation. However, while the application took some time to be heard and was hard-fought at all stages, I am not prepared to say that that any impugned conduct is sufficient to warrant enhanced costs. 7 Other factors to be considered in relation to the fairness of enhanced costs include the fact that no multiplier was requested or granted in relation to the two previous costs awards in this case: one in favor of each party. Further, a court should consider whether significantly enhanced costs at the preliminary stage may have a disproportionately negative impact on the progress of a filed action. 8 For these reasons no multiplier is granted …. For an example of Rule 10.32 being applied, see: Elder Advocates of Alberta Society v. Alberta, 2020 ABQB 54, 2020 CarswellAlta 96, 96 C.C.L.I. (5th) 236; appeal dismissed 2021 ABCA 67.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.33 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) In making a costs award, the Court may consider all or any of the following: (a) the result of the action and the degree of success of each party; (b) the amount claimed and the amount recovered; (c) the importance of the issues; (d) the complexity of the action; (e) the apportionment of liability; (f) the conduct of a party that tended to shorten the action; (g) any other matter related to the question of reasonable and proper costs that the Court considers appropriate. (2) In deciding whether to impose, deny or vary an amount in a costs award, the Court may consider all or any of the following: (a) the conduct of a party that was unnecessary or that unnecessarily lengthened or delayed the action or any stage or step of the action; (b) a party's denial of or refusal to admit anything that should have been admitted; (c) whether a party started separate actions for claims that should have been filed in one action or whether a party unnecessarily separated that party's defence from that of another party; (d) whether any application, proceeding or step in an action was unnecessary, improper or a mistake; (e) an irregularity in a commencement document, pleading, affidavit, notice, prescribed form or document; (f) a contravention of or non-compliance with these rules or an order; (g) whether a party has engaged in misconduct. (h) any offer of settlement made, regardless of whether or not the offer of settlement complies with Part 4, Division 5. Alta. Reg. 36/2020, s. 15

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.33 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.33:1 Rule 10.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.33. 1. Evidence in Costs Applications In Mitran v. Guarantee RV Centre Inc. (1999), 72 Alta. L.R. (3d) 54 (Q.B.), counsel made submissions to the court as the “reasonableness” of certain costs being sought. In the course of those submissions he made certain assertions of fact not found in the evidence. In determining that those assertions by counsel could not be considered as evidence, Johnstone J. held, at p. 62, that “the evidence available on the costs application is restricted to sworn evidence” because “any submissions he made were merely hearsay.” 2. “Reasonableness” When considering the reasonableness or otherwise of an expenditure made by the defendant I must view the matter through the eyes of the defendant and in light of the problem facing it when the expenditure was made. The test of reasonableness is not, in my opinion, entirely based on the importance of the expenditure to success at trial. Hindsight may show that some liabilities assumed were, in the end, of little or no benefit. The question is whether the expense was reasonable and proper in the light of the circumstances which existed at the time it was incurred. The issues raised from time to time by the pleadings and by discovery and production are significant circumstances. The magnitude of the expenditure in relation to the amount at risk in the proceedings is another important consideration. In all cases the party taxing costs has the burden of showing that both the nature of the expense and its amount were reasonable and proper in the circumstances. Petrogas Processing Ltd. v. Westcoast Transmission Co. (1990), 105 A.R. 384 (Q.B.), at 394, per O'Leary J. Madam Justice Johnstone in MacCabe v. Westlock Roman Catholic Separate School District No. 110 (1999), 70 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (Q.B.); additional reasons at (1999) 73 Alta. L.R. (3d) 107 (Q.B.), at pp. 22–23, set forth the following factors to consider when assessing the reasonableness of a claimed disbursement: It is clear that an award for disbursements is within my discretion. In determining whether or not a disbursement is reasonable, I may consider the following factors: (a) the length of the trial; (b) its complexity; (c) the nature and number of the issues involved in the trial; (d) the degree of contest as to evidentiary matters; (e) the degree of contest as to credibility of witnesses, including professional expert witnesses; (f) the nature and number of the defenses mounted; (g) the requirement for and use of experts; (h) the use of models, tests and scientific evidence; (i) the nature and amount of damages at issue; (j) the relationship of the expeses claimed as costs to the amounts at issue in damages; (k) any agreement of counsel to share specific expense items. Her Ladyship then quoted with approval O'Leary J.'s statement in Petrogas Processing Ltd. v. Westcoast Transmission Co. (1990), 105 A.R. 384 (Q.B.) (reproduced above). She said that “the overriding consideration therefore is the reasonableness of the disbursement in light of the circumstances which existed at the time it was incurred” (p. 23). At p. 30 she relied on the following statement of Leggat J. in Morrissette v. Smith (1990), 39 C.P.C. (2d) 30 (B.C. S.C.): [the] Test was whether, at the time the expense was incurred, it was a proper disbursement in the sense of not being extravagant, negligent, mistaken or the result of excessive caution or excessive zeal, judged by the situation at the time when the expense was incurred. 3. Unnecessary litigation For a list of actions which have been found to constitute “unnecessary litigation”[Rule 10.33(2)d)], please see Condominium Corporation No 022 5899 v. 499430 Alberta Ltd, 2020 ABQB 233, 2020 CarswellAlta 625 at paragraphs 59–61. 4. Discretion with Respect to Costs In Chisholm v. Lindsay, 2015 ABCA 179, the Court said: 44 As we see it, the purpose of the Rules of Court is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly, justly and expeditiously resolved either by a Court process in a timely and cost-effective way or in some other fashion, as the Rules contemplate. In every case, the relevant inquiry will be whether there was a legitimate attempt to settle given the issues in dispute and mindful of the conduct of the litigation. Such an approach encourages settlements without derogating from that referred to as the foundation of the formal Rules. Maheasserts that notwithstanding strict compliance with the formal Rules of Court, a trial judge must be permitted to take account, in the context of other factors, of non-compliant offers made in good faith to settle litigation. The first matter is to consider the Court's discretionary rights … the Court has a wide area of discretion in awarding costs under R. 601 of the Alberta Rules of Court. See also s. 19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. C-29. Although the Court's discretion in ordering costs is traditionally very wide, it is not a discretion without bounds with the scope of such discretion being recently discussed by Mason J. in Pharand Ski Corp. v. Alberta (1991), [81 Alta. L.R. (2d) 304] (Q.B.), at p. 398: While the court has a wide discretion when awarding costs, the discretion must be exercised judicially and in accordance with established principles. This broad discretion comes from, and is based upon the absolute discretion vested in the Court of Chancery in England with respect to costs. As such, it is to be exercised in accordance with the precepts and historical precedents established by that court and developed therefrom, by case law based upon a proper application and extension of those precedents. See Andrews v. Barnes (1887), 39 Ch. D. 133 and Mobil Oil of Canada Limited v. Canadian Superior Oil Limited and Neilsen, supra. Claudio's Restaurant Group Inc. v. Calgary (City) (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 141 (Q.B.), at 147–48, per Rooke J. In Papaschase Indian Band No. 136 v. Canada (Attorney General) (2004), 45 Alta. L.R. (4th) 72 (Q.B.), Slatter J. reviewed the discretion which may be exercised in matters of costs. At p. 79, his Lordship said: The Court of Appeal in [Pauli v. ACE INA Insurance (2005), 1 W.W.R. 12 (Alta. C.A.)] recognized the usual rule that costs follow the event. However, the Court held that this normal rule can be displaced when some or all of the following factors are present: (a) the decision resolves a new or unsettled point, and it was in the public interest that the point be settled. In such cases it is relevant whether the litigants have a direct pecuniary interest in the proceedings, and whether the issue extends beyond the immediate interests of the parties. While the Court recognized that all decisions have some precedential value, and that that did not mean that all litigation was in the public interest, it concluded that settling the point in the Pauli action was of public interest. (b) Costs may not follow the event if a novel point is involved. The Court held that the interpretation of the standard form of insurance contract at issue in Pauli raised a novel point. (c) The Court also concluded that Pauli was a test case, which is another reason to depart from the normal costs rule. While the class in Pauli was defined so widely that it would cover every person in Alberta with a similar claim, the Court held that the decision might prove persuasive in other similar actions. (d) The Court noted that class actions were permitted in order to increase access to justice, and that exposing plaintiffs to costs would discourage meritorious class actions. The Court noted that the representative plaintiffs could have expected to gain no more than $1,000.00 each if they had been successful, but they were now subject to a costs award of $115,000.00 to $125,000.00. Bowes v. Edmonton (City) (2005), 49 Alta. L.R. (4th) 100 (Q.B.) is an interesting example of a court exercising its discretion regarding costs. The Plaintiffs sued the City of Edmonton, alleging negligence and nuisance. The City successfully defended the claims on the basis that the Plaintiffs had commenced their action beyond the limitation period, though the Court determined that the City had been negligent. At pp. 101–102, Clackson J. made the following statements about the action: The City filed offers of judgment in September 2004 and withdrew those offers in December 2004. The vast bulk of the time and expense which these cases consumed related to everything but limitation periods. The usual rule is that costs follow the event. However, the Plaintiffs argue that the Limitations Act resulted in an unjust and unfair deprivation of otherwise sound claims. Therefore, the Plaintiffs argue that costs should be used as a means of ameliorating the inequity. I agree that the Plaintiffs have been unfairly deprived. That unfairness is however not attributable in any way to the City, it is inherent in limitations law and ultimate limitation periods. There are instances where costs are awarded against a successful party. However, that result usually occurs where the successful party has been guilty of some misconduct that warrants censure. The City is guilty of no misconduct in this case. The inequity here is statutory in origin. Therefore, there is no good reason why the usual rule should be departed from in this case. … Having found that the Defendant was guilty of no misconduct, having found any “unfairness” in result was a consequence of the nature of limitation date statutes, and having found “no good reason” to depart from the usual rule, Clackson J. then said (at p. 102): … However, it is appropriate in my view to analyze the result more particularly than simply who won and who lost. As I have said, this trial was dominated by issues of negligence and nuisance. The vast bulk of the evidence and effort was directed at the issue of negligence. The Plaintiffs were successful in that regard. The matter of the Plaintiffs' nuisance claims were based in large measure upon the evidence and arguments relating to the negligence claims. The City successfully defended itself on the nuisance claims. In my view, a costs award should reflect all of those results and the history of the action to the date of trial. As well the costs award should reflect the fact that the Plaintiffs did not achieve a result that “beat” the offer made by the City prior to trial. Finally, the costs award should reflect the relative expenditure of time and effort on the individual issues which were in dispute. Having regard to all of those factors, I award one set of costs on Column 5 of Schedule C of the Rules of Court to the Plaintiffs for all steps taken up to December 2, 2004. Thereafter I award the Plaintiffs 70% of one set of costs on Column 5 through to and including the trial and the determination of costs. The Plaintiffs' proper disbursements are awarded to them in full. I award the City 30% of one set of double costs on Column 5 from December 2, 2004 through the trial and the determination of costs. The City's proper disbursements are awarded to them in full. Both sides are entitled to include second counsel fee in their Bills of Costs. The unusual end result is that the successful Defendant, who properly relied on the limitation statute enacted by the Legislature, was guilty of no misconduct in the action, and had made a formal offer of settlement which was not accepted by the Plaintiff, was ordered to pay to the unsuccessful Plaintiffs costs up to the date of the withdrawal of the defence settlement offer, and was itself only awarded 30% of its double costs after the date of the withdrawal. The rationale for the decision seems to have been that the majority of the trial was directed at the issue of negligence which the Plaintiffs established but the Defendant avoided the consequences of that finding because the limitation statute gave the defendant immunity. However, the decision does effectively penalize the Defendant for simply relying on legislation (Limitations Act) the provisions of which the Legislature passed having determined what was a proper balance between those seeking redress for wrongs and those who must defend themselves against claims. In Lee v. Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board) (2005), 386 A.R. 86 (Q.B.), Hillier J. said, at p. 101: The Court may exercise its discretion to deny costs where there is (1) misconduct either before or after the lawsuit, (2) miscarriage in the procedure or (3) oppressive and vexatious conduct of proceedings…. In 1022049 Alberta Ltd. v. Medicine Hat (City), 2006 ABQB 208, 2006 CarswellAlta 749, 400 A.R. 245, 29 C.P.C. (6th) 342, Erb J. considered whether the Court should consider post-judgment evidence when determining costs. At p. 250, her Ladyship said: 15 Post hearing evidence relating to the merits or conduct of a party should not be considered unless there is clear connection between that evidence and the proceedings. For example, post hearing evidence of fraudulent conduct such as deliberately misleading the court could be considered in determining costs regardless of which party was successful at trial. 16 The rules of evidence apply to a costs hearing. The Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook at p. 576 notes that “inadmissible material cannot be looked at by the court, even when considering costs.” In Anderson v. Amoco Canada Oil & Gas, [2002] A.J. No. 829, (2002 ABCA 162 at para. 61), it was stated: The trial judge directed that costs be paid by the appellants forthwith rather than at the conclusion of the proceedings. She made this direction on the basis of her finding that the appellants were being funded by a corporation which had been formed for the purpose of pursuing the litigation. The trial judge's understanding resulted from her reference to correspondence between Wheatland Resources Ltd. and individuals who are not parties to the proceedings. This correspondence was not part of the evidence at trial. It was attached to the post-trial submission of counsel for one of the petroleum owners on costs. It was not properly before the trial judge, and she erred in referring to it. We nevertheless agree with the trial judge that this is an appropriate case for directing payment of costs forthwith. [emphasis added] 17 The Supreme Court of Canada affirmed the Court of Appeal's decision, including costs: [2004] 2 S.C.R. 3, per Major J., at para. 43. Erb J. then said, at p. 250: 19 The post hearing conduct of the City is also irrelevant to the matter of costs granted in the original Applications. As such, it is inadmissible. In 642718 Alberta Ltd. v. Alberta (Minister of Public Works, Supply & Services), 2005 ABQB 810, 2005 CarswellAlta 1607, 390 A.R. 193, 56 Alta. L.R. (4th) 192, Read, J. held that pre-litigation conduct could be considered when exercising the court's discretion about costs. At p. 199, Read, J. said: …I am satisfied that a successful party may be deprived of costs or have varied costs that would otherwise be payable because of pre-litigation conduct in some circumstances. … Also see the annotation “Conduct of Parties as ‘Special Reason’” under Rule 4.29. In Jones v. Gerosa, 2016 ABQB 614, 2016 CarswellAlta 2140, 45 Alta. L.R. (6th) 243, Justice Graesser made these comments: 31 In Schwartz Estate v Myron, 2013 ABQB 147, I discussed the principles relating to cost awards in Alberta at para 111: The minutia of the evidence is rarely the deciding factor in a claim for costs. Courts will normally take a bigger picture view of costs, following the basic principles that: 1. Costs follow the event; 2. Usual costs are those provided for in Schedule C of the Rules of Court; 3. The Court has a wide discretion (to be exercised judicially) as to the awarding of costs in any matter; 4. A successful party may be denied costs, or awarded costs on a lesser scale, because of his or her conduct during the course of the litigation, or because of the magnitude of the award in comparison with the costs calculated on the usual column. 32 I repeat what I said in Schwartz Estate at paras 251 and 252: [251] In my view, the courts need to take care to avoid cost proceedings being as lengthy and costly as the underlying litigation. It is not an appropriate use of scarce judicial resources, whether it be review or assessment officers, masters or judges, to have them pore over lawyers' time records, pleadings, questioning transcripts, briefs and trial proceedings to determine whether a particular party misconducted itself during some step in the litigation. Hindsight always provides clarity, and looking back, it may be relatively easy to say that a particular position was ill conceived, a particular application was unnecessary, it was not necessary or helpful to have third counsel involved at an application or proceeding, a brief was too long and detailed, a witness was not necessary, and the like. [252] It is not the intent of cost proceedings to retry cases or revisit each hour of lawyer time logged on the file to determine whether the time was well spent and proportionate to the nature and magnitude of the litigation. 33 I also commented at paragraph 203: [203] I do not view the principle regarding denial of costs because of misconduct during the litigation as a basis to review every step in the action and every position being taken by counsel throughout the course of litigation. The intent of the cost rules and Schedule C in particular is to make the assessment of costs routine other than in exceptional circumstances. 34 It is also not the focus of a cost hearing to relitigate the case. I would also add that no authority needs to be cited for the general principle in Alberta that the loser pays. 35 I would also observe that when assessing costs when there is a claim and a counterclaim, the Court generally “nets” the two to determine who the ultimate winner is. That is clear from cases such as Wilde v. Archean Energy Ltd., 2008 ABCA 132. There, the Court stated at paragraph 9: Generally the costs follow the ultimate result, and costs are not usually apportioned on an issue-by-issue basis, a claim-by-claim basis or on a head-of-damages basis, although there is a discretion to do so in proper cases: Sutherland v. Canada (Attorney General), 2008 BCCA 27 (CanLII) at para. 7; British Columbia v. Worthington (Canada) Inc., 1988 CanLII 175 (BC CA), [1989] 1 W.W.R. 1, 29 B.C.L.R. (2d) 145, 32 C.P.C. (2d) 166 (B.C.C.A.); Portugal Cove-St. Phillips (Town) v. Willcott, (1997), 1997 CanLII 14702 (NL CA), 150 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 183, 20 C.P.C. (4th) 237 (Nfld. C.A.) at paras. 13–19. 36 That is not automatic, as there are circumstances where it may be appropriate to award costs on each of the claim and counterclaim, or on an issue-by-issue basis, as was done in Clarke v Syncrude Canada Ltd., 2014 ABQB 430. 37 In Herman v Delong (# 2), 1999 ABQB 745, Veit J observed at paragraph 5: [5] Success in legal proceedings, at least as a measure of costs, is to be determined objectively. Garneau Lofts Inc. (2005), 59 Alta. L.R. (4th) 255 (Q.B.), Slatter J. (as he then was), at pp. 258–264, gave the following summary of the concept of “thrown away costs”: The concept of “thrown away costs” arises because in Alberta our system of civil procedure is largely “prejudice-based”. A failure to comply with the Rules will generally not be fatal so long as any prejudice to the other side can be remedied by an award of costs, an adjournment, or some other type of relief. This general rule has many manifestations, but some of the more specific ones are: (a) a missed deadline in the Rules will not be fatal if any prejudice can be remedied by costs. (b) if a judgment is entered or a step is taken in default of appearance of one of the parties, the step taken in default can often be opened up. (c) if a pleading is for some reason deficient or inadequate, an amendment will generally be allowed, so long as there is no prejudice that cannot be remedied. (d) late applications for adjournments of scheduled court appearances will often be granted, again so long as any prejudice can be remedied in some way. This prejudice-based system of proceedings has been criticized on the basis that it is too unstructured, and it leads to delay and added expense. Nevertheless, it remains the general rule governing civil practice in Alberta. Apart from the general principle that procedural missteps that can be remedied will not be fatal, there are some specific rules relating to particular types of missteps. Without attempting to state in detail the law or the tests applicable, some examples include: (a) there are some specific Rules, such as Rules 190 and 538(4), which deal with the consequences of missing specific time requirements in the Rules. (b) in opening up a noting in default, the moving party must generally provide some explanation for non-appearance, must show that the application to open up was brought promptly, and must demonstrate a triable defence. (c) as a general rule, Rule 141 provides that an amending party is not entitled to costs of the amendment of a pleading. (This Rule is perhaps somewhat academic given the repeal of the specific item in Schedule “C” that used to allow a separate fee for amendment of pleadings.) (d) where a late adjournment is granted, costs will often be awarded for wasted preparation, keeping in mind that not all preparation will be completely lost. In any of these situations, “thrown away costs” may be awarded as a method of negating any prejudice that might otherwise fall on the responding party. What costs are “thrown away” will depend on the particular type of application being brought, and the cases must be examined to see the particular context in which they were decided.8 In dealing with what are truly “thrown away costs”, all of these procedural situations break down into two parts: (a) there is initially some procedural misstep by the applicant party, be that the faulty drafting of a pleading, the failure to attend in court on the appropriate date, the failure to be ready to proceed on a scheduled trial date, or the missing of a deadline. This procedural misstep causes the responding party to take some step (such as getting a default judgment, preparing for a trial that is adjourned, or responding to the faulty pleading), or perhaps it may simply cause delay and require an application to comply with the Rules (in the case of a missed deadline). When the applicant later tries to correct its misstep, the action taken by the respondent becomes “wasted” or “thrown away”. (b) the second step is then to resolve whether the applicant who made the misstep is entitled to some relief. At this stage of the proceedings, the applicant who committed the procedural misstep alleges that he or she is within the general rule that missteps are allowed so long as there is no prejudice that is not remediable in some way. The respondent might concede that the applicant has met the test, or may assert that the applicant is not entitled to relief, and resist the application. There may then be a contested proceeding over whether the applicant is entitled to relief. … Thrown Away Costs There is conflicting case law on the concept of thrown away costs. There are two competing philosophies. The first is that the applicant who made the misstep is seeking an indulgence, and must pay all the costs of seeking the indulgence, even if it is clear on the authorities that the applicant is entitled to the indulgence: Fox v. Bourget (1987), 17 C.P.C. (2d) 94 (Ont. Dist. Ct.) citing Aliferis v. Parfeniuk (1985), 1 C.P.C. (2d) 41, 9 O.A.C. 215 (Ont. C.A.), although Aliferis does not appear to state any general principle to that effect. In the leading case of Burgoine v. Taylor (1878), 9 Ch. D. 1 (Eng. Ch. Div.) a judgment was entered in default of appearance due to an error by a solicitor. The Defendant was initially unsuccessful in opening up the judgment, but succeeded on appeal, where Jessel, M.R. said: Solicitors cannot, any more than other men, conduct their business without sometimes making slips; and where a solicitor watches the list, and happens to miss the case, in consequence of which it is taken in his absence, it is in accordance with justice and with the course of practice to restore the action to the paper, on the terms of the party in default paying the costs of the day, which include all costs thrown away by reason of the trial becoming abortive. As a general rule, solicitors in my branch of the Court consent to such an order as is now asked, and that such an application should be opposed is to me a novelty. Still, as the Appellant was in default, he must pay the costs of the application to the Court below, but no costs of the appeal. Thus, the applicant had to pay costs, even though he was successful, and entitled to the relief according to the practice of the Court. Other cases have followed a more functional approach, under which only the costs that are truly wasted are payable. Smith v. Harrington (1994), 36 C.P.C. (3d) 209 (Ont. Gen. Div.) followed this approach, citing Royal Bank v. Blatt (1991), 26 A.C.W.S. (3d) 926 (Ont. Gen. Div.): An award of costs thrown away is to compensate the party for the work done in preparing for a trial that did not occur. I agree with the following statement adopted by Assessment Officer Conover in Nippa v. C.H. Lewis (Lucan Ltd.), January 28, 1988, unreported, that: …costs thrown away on a solicitor and client scale is intended to result in full indemnity for all steps which were reasonably necessary to proceed with the action but which have been rendered useless by the other party's conduct in responding or not responding to the action. This approach has the advantage of discouraging the respondent from opposing relief that the applicant is entitled to, because the respondent will get costs of the motion even if unsuccessful, as happened in Burgoine v. Taylor. The dispute, at its root, is whether the rule that the successful party is prima facie entitled to costs applies. On the one hand, if the applicant asserts a right to fix an error, and wins in the face of resistence to that relief, the applicant should get costs. On the other hand, it is asserted that the party who made the error should pay, because it caused the problem and is seeking an indulgence. … The Court of Queen's Bench Costs Manual, prepared by the Taxing Officers, defines “thrown away costs” as follows: “Thrown Away Costs” Are those that a party would not have incurred save for the actions of another party. The most common would be the costs awarded a Plaintiff upon the successful setting aside of his/her default judgment. Consider the following: Item # Description Thrown Away Cost? 1 Pleadings (drafting, filing & serving Statement of Claim) no 6(2) Ex Parte Application for a Substitutional Service Order no 1 Noting in Default (a component of Item 1—get a proportion yes of the Item) 2 Uncontested Assessment Application yes 5 Examination on Affidavit re: application to set aside default yes judgment 7(1) Defence of Application to Set Aside Default Judgment yes The Manual treats as thrown away not only the wasted effort of the respondent, but also the steps taken by the applicant to determine if it has a right to correct the original error.18 The general pattern in these cases is that when a party makes a procedural misstep, that party will then assert to the respondent that it has the right to correct that misstep if it eliminates all the prejudice. For example, it may assert that it has the right to amend a defective pleading, on payment of the costs of any wasted effort by the respondent. It might assert a right to open up a noting in default, because it has met the legal test for doing that (supra, para. 7(b)), again on payment of wasted costs. The respondent can do one of two things: it can acknowledge that the applicant has the right to fix the misstep, because the applicable test has been met, including that any prejudice can be eliminated on appropriate terms, or it can deny that the applicant has the right to correct the misstep. In the latter situation, a new sub-dispute is created. There is now an issue as to whether the appropriate test (e.g. to amend, to adjourn, to open up noting in default, etc.) has been met. When this issue is litigated, the general rule should be that costs follow the event, subject of course to the Court's general jurisdiction over costs. Granting costs to an unsuccessful party only encourages unreasonable opposition to relief to which the applicant is entitled. Therefore, as a general rule where (for example) one party asserts a right to amend pleadings, and the other party denies that right, and the amending party must take the matter to court, costs should follow the event. If the applicant succeeds in its motion to amend, it should get costs. Rule 141 says simply that the amending party must bear the costs of the amendment (as I have previously mentioned, supra, para. 7(c), a reference to a now repealed part of Schedule “C”). Rule 141 does not say that the applicant must pay the costs of the fight over whether it has the right to amend, even if it wins that fight. That would be a most undesirable result, because it would mean that the respondents on motions like that could defend them with impunity, knowing that win or lose they would receive costs. Absent some positive misconduct, the successful moving party should get costs of the motion to permit the amendment. Likewise, if a party is noted in default, but asserts that it has met the test for opening up a default, it should be entitled to costs if successful. If the respondent denies that the defaulting party has the right to open up the default, and forces the matter to Chambers, then costs should follow the event. Again, it would be an undesirable result to allow respondents to defend such applications regardless of the merits of the applicant's position. The applicant may have caused the noting in default, but it did not cause the subsequent court battle about whether it was entitled to open up the noting in default. With applications to adjourn, a distinction should be drawn between the effort that will be wasted if there is an adjournment, and the dispute over the right to an adjournment. In principle, if the applicant asserts a right to adjournment, and under the prevailing rules and practice the applicant is entitled to that adjournment, then if the respondent resists, costs should follow the event. However, if the adjournment is the result of some fault of the applicant, the applicant is often required to pay the costs of the adjournment application, even if successful. This is an exception to Rule 607. It should be noted that in these situations the costs of determining whether the applicant is entitled to be relieved of its procedural misstep is not really “wasted”. There is a dispute over the rights of the applicant to relief from its error, and the application resolves that dispute. Those efforts are not “wasted”, because the dispute must be resolved. Furthermore, those proceedings are not a direct result of the procedural misstep of the applicant; they are really brought on by the respondent's failure to accept that the applicant has made out its right to be relieved of the consequence of its procedural misstep. Where the applicant is entitled to relief the respondent should not unreasonably litigate the point. As a result, the rule that costs go to the successful party (Rule 607) should prevail over any rule about “wasted” costs. In summary, a distinction should be drawn between: (a) the costs of the wasted work caused by the procedural misstep that is the source of the problem, and (b) litigating the dispute over whether the person who took the misstep has the right to fix it. The principle that the Rules are prejudice-based, and that procedural errors should be forgiven if prejudice can be eliminated, must be balanced against the other rule that costs generally go to the successful party: Rule 607. Subject to the overriding discretion of the judge over costs, only the first category of costs (paragraph (a)) are “thrown away”. 15. Purpose of Costs I am aware that the principle and purpose behind the wording of party-and-party costs is to provide indemnity to the person entitled to them Such Rules of Court are not designed for the purpose of punishing, penalizing or benefitting a party to an action. In Alberta, except in unique circumstances, party-and-party costs will not approach indemnification of the successful party and thus it is more accurate to describe the awarding of costs as a contribution toward the successful party's expense in prosecuting or defending the action. Wenden v. Trikha (1992), 1 Alta L.R. (3d) 283 (Q.B.), at 293, per Murray J. And McDonald J. said: While the allocation of costs of a lawsuit is always in the discretion of the court, the exercise of that discretion must be consistent with established principles and practice. It is traditionally accepted in Canada's common law provinces that as a general rule the successful party recovers its costs from the unsuccessful party. However, such recovery is normally on a party-and-party basis. That is, the costs recoverable are those fees fixed for the steps in the proceeding by a schedule of fees (Sched. C. in Alberta's Rules of Court), plus reasonable disbursements. It is not intended that the successful party receive full indemnification of those fees and disbursements which it would be charged by its counsel. In England the degree of indemnification appears to be considerably higher than is normal in Canada. In almost all jurisdictions of the United States of America the rule is that no costs are recoverable by the successful party. The Canadian practice reflects an attempt to balance two conflicting interests. On the one hand, it is argued that if a party is successful and there are no circumstances constituting blameworthiness in the conduct of the litigation by that party, it is unfair to require the successful party to bear any costs incurred by his counsel in prosecuting or defending the action. On the other hand, it is argued that if the unsuccessful party is required to bear all the costs of the successful party, citizens will be unduly hesitant to sue to assert their rights (even valid ones) or to defend their rights when sued. The partial indemnity practice as it exists in Canada is a compromise intended to give some scope in practice for each of the conflicting policy considerations. When the case is of considerable magnitude and complexity, the practice in Alberta contemplates that the court may order the unsuccessful party to pay a multiple of the fees that are fixed by Sched. C. But even then it is not intended that there be full indemnity, except in extraordinary circumstances. Reese v. Alberta (1993), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 (Q.B.), at 44–45, per McDonald J. 16. Consider Complexity and Difficulty of Proceedings In addition to s. 19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act and the relevant Rules of Court, McCarthy v. Bd. of Trustees, supra, is authority for the proposition that the difficulty and complexity of the proceedings are relevant in considering the scale of party-party costs to be awarded. Similarly, in the Alberta Court of Appeal case of Calbar Securities Ltd. v. Toole Peet Co. (1984), 30 Alta. L.R. (2d) 286 … which upheld the trial judge's award of costs on triple col. 5 with no limiting rule to apply, the late McGillivray C.J.A. held at pp. 287–88: The court is of the opinion that the scale of costs and the exclusion of the limiting rule cannot be based on the number of parties who are to pay the costs, but should depend upon the amount involved, the complexity and importance of the issues, and the length of trial. In New Brunswick, the Court of Appeal in Williams v. New Brunswick; St. John v. Williams; Chubb Indust. Ltd. v. St. John (1985), 34 C.C.L.T. 299 at 320 … held that, although the amount recovered in a lawsuit has always been important, it … is not the sole criterion and in fixing costs the Court may consider other matters including the complexity of the proceedings, the importance of the issues, the conduct of the parties, the manner in which the proceedings were conducted and any other matter relevant to the question of costs. Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1987), 50 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 (Q.B.), at 10–11, per Wachowich J. 17. When punitive damages have been awarded In Indutech Canada Ltd. v. Gibbs Pipe Distributors Ltd., 2012 ABQB 425, 2012 CarswellAlta 1909, 84 Alta. L.R. (5th) 55, the successful Plaintiffs sought enhanced costs. The defendants submitted that since punitive damages had been awarded against them, costs should not be enhanced. Madam Justice Romaine disagreed, and, at paragraphs 11–12, said: 11 The Gibbs Group Defendants submit that where a party has been punished for misconduct by an award of punitive damages, as was the case here, courts have been disinclined to punish that party further through a costs award: 539618 Ontario Ltd. v. Stathopoulos (1989), 17 A.C.W.S. (3d) 159 (Ont.H.C.J.) at para. 8. 12 It may be more accurate to say that an award of punitive damages may be a factor in considering enhanced costs, since the rules and case authority in Alberta do not preclude the consideration of misconduct at the costs stage of proceedings, whether or not punitive damages have been found to be appropriate. Punitive damages reflect the misconduct of the Gibbs Group Defendants over the course of the Agency Agreement. An enhanced costs award reflects misconduct during the course of the litigation, and there is evidence of such misconduct in the findings of credibility made with respect to various of the Gibbs Group Defendants. Justice Romaine's decision was unsuccessfully appealed (Indutech Canada Ltd. v. Gibbs Pipe Distributors Ltd., 2013 ABCA 111, 2013 CarswellAlta 957, 544 A.R. 205, 82 Alta. L.R. (5th) 217). The Court said, at paragraphs 100, and 102–106: 100 In a companion appeal, the appellants appeal the trial judge's awarded enhanced costs under some categories available under Column 5 of Schedule C of the Rules of Court. They do not contest the award of enhanced costs in relation to other categories. Her award elevated the costs payable by the appellants above the $285,000 which would have otherwise been ordered paid by them. … 102 She rejected the argument that enhanced costs should not be awarded because the harm they addressed was met by the award of punitive damages. Her award was grounded in the nature of the litigation itself. She accepted that an award of punitive damages should reflect misconduct prior to the commencement of the litigation and of enhanced costs misconduct during the course of the litigation; see Polar Ice Express Inc v Arctic Glacier Inc, 2009 ABCA 20 at paras 21–22, 446 AR 295. She found such misconduct “in the findings of credibility” made with respect to various of the [appellants], notwithstanding that she then proceeded to give specific reasons for each enhancement which did not rest on this finding of misconduct. 103 No authority precludes an award of enhanced costs because punitive damages were also awarded in the proper case. Judges have, in some cases, declined to make such an award upon concluding that remedies given, including punitive damages, were sufficient to account for the wrongdoing of the unsuccessful party. The trial judge implicitly concluded otherwise, from her comments relating to her findings of litigation misconduct. 104 Similarly, while some judges have declined to find litigation misconduct simply because of credibility findings made against certain witnesses, no authority precludes the award for that reason. In any event, the nature and depth of the negative credibility findings made against the appellants' witnesses elevates this case from the more typical situation where a trial judge simply accepts the evidence of one witness over that of others. For example, the appellants produced 11 separate affidavits of records. There was evidence that preparation for questioning took an inordinate amount of time because the transgressions could be uncovered only through detailed examination of these records, encompassing between 15,000 to 20,000 pages of documents produced by the appellants. 105 The enhanced costs award would have been justified here simply on the basis of the complexity and duration of the ligation, without reference to litigation misconduct. That practice is often followed by a judge electing to give a multiple of the appropriate column in Schedule C to reflect atypical or extraordinary aspects in the procedure leading up to judgment in a given matter. This consideration more than offsets any concern of double-compensation arising from the award of punitive damages for pre-litigation conduct. 106 The trial judge's award of enhanced costs lay well within her properly exercised discretion; see Court of Queen's Bench Act, RSA 2000, c C-31, s 21. 18. Adjournments I assume that when the bar decided to adopt the amounts set out in item 25 of the tariff, it had in mind that these are the costs that would be awarded, except in exceptional circumstances… … It is only where the parties make out a special case for additional costs that an amount other than the tariff amount should be awarded. It may well be appropriate to take into account “fault”in relation to the need for an adjournment in determining if something other than the tariff item should be applied. For example, if the party whose action necessitated the adjournment was somehow “at fault”, it may be entirely appropriate to award thrown away costs, or even punitive costs. However, where there is no “fault”, and there are no exceptional circumstances the tariff should apply. Lines v. Brink (1994), 24 Alta. L.R. (3d) 227 (Q.B.), at 238–39, per Veit J. 19. Compassion is Not a Factor In P. (S.F.) v. MacDonald (1999), 242 A.R. 134 (Q.B.), an unsuccessful plaintiff sought relief from the provisions of R 605(5). At p. 142, Veit J. said: The plaintiff asks for the court's compassion. However, the adoption of the plaintiff's argument would result in a deprivation perpetrated on the defendants. It is inappropriate, therefore, to say that compassion is an appropriate factor. It seems to me, rather, that fairness and equity are the benchmarks here. By those standards, it is fair to apply the provisions of rule 605(5) which provisions were known to the plaintiff before she opened the trial. 20. Costs in Estate Litigation In Chabros v. Anderson, 2012 ABQB 517, 2012 CarswellAlta 1422, 79 E.T.R. (3d) 317, Justice Clark considered Rules 10.33(1) and (2). He said, at paragraphs 6–15: 6 These are the rules which govern in, for lack of better term, “ordinary” civil litigation. However, both parties pointed out that costs are treated differently in estate litigation. The Executors referred to the “historical” and “modern” approaches to costs in estate litigation. 7 Historically, it was common practice in estate matters for courts to award costs of all parties out of the estate. This approach, however, has been out of favour for several years. As noted by Graesser J. of this Court in Re Foote Estate, 2010 ABQB 197 at para. 16, the “modern” approach to costs in estate litigation “requires careful scrutiny of the litigation to restrict unwarranted litigation and protect estates from being depleted by such litigation.” In more recent years, the courts have recognized that awards of costs operate to the detriment of estate beneficiaries. See, inter alia, Babchuk v. Kutz, 2007 ABQB 88 and my own reasons in Johnson v. Beers, 1999 ABQB 723, 252 AR 187. Thus, the general approach now in estate litigation is that costs follow the event unless the challenge to the will was reasonable or an exception can be justified on public policy grounds. 8 Of course, this case did not concern a challenge to the validity of the Will or proceedings to determine its proper construction. Rather, the points at issue are the proper compensation payable to the Executors for their administration of the Estate and, as a related matter, the Executors' right to be indemnified for expenses reasonably and properly incurred in the course of administration. The Executors rely upon this statement from Jennifer J. Jenkins, Compensation & Duties of Estate Trustees, Guardians & Attorneys (Toronto: Canada Law Book, 2011) at para. 22:20.20: It should be appreciated that any discussion contrasting the traditional approach to costs with the developing mindset is too simple an analysis. The issue of costs has its own particular slant, depending on the type of litigation, which hinges primarily on the role of the estate trustee. For example, a contested passing of accounts is considered to be a significant part of the administration of an estate. Thus an estate trustee is entitled to take an adversarial position in defence of his or her administration and claim for compensation and, generally speaking, the starting point is that the estate trustee and the beneficiaries are awarded costs as a legitimate expense of the estate. 9 The Executors also referred to the following comments from Donald J. (as he then was) in Re Kanee Estate (1991) 41 ETR 263 (BCSC) at paras. 17, 23, 24 and 26: There is much force in the argument advanced by Mr. Wilson that when remuneration is the only issue, the executors are acting in their own self-interest and not for the benefit of the estate and, therefore, they and any contending parties should be treated as ordinary litigants as far as costs are concerned. He endeavours to support this proposition by a decision of the Saskatchewan Surrogate Court in Re Preboy Estate (1989), 72 Sask. R. 33 (Surr. Ct.), aff'd (1989), 74 Sask. R. 223 (C.A.), where at p. 43 [72 Sask. R.] McLellan J. said: There can be no justification for the solicitors charging the beneficiaries a fee to research the law to find out what they and the executors are entitled to charge the estate. … The litigation model does not, in my opinion, fit the circumstances of this case. Executors do not step outside the estate to deal with the question of remuneration; the subject is customarily dealt with as part of the passing-of-accounts process. This is so because of the intimate connection it has with the estate. I cannot agree with Re Preboy, supra, if it purports to lay down a statement of general principle. The Court in that case did not elaborate any reasons for the statement quoted above. It is inapplicable to the case at Bar because, as the Master rightly held, it is inappropriate to set up an adversity in interest between the estate and the executors in the settlement of remuneration. Subject to considerations of reasonableness and honesty, the question of costs should be dealt with in the same way for remuneration as for the other aspects in the passing of accounts. Executors are entitled to be paid for their work. … The questioning of remuneration should not be considered in any way analogous to such truly litigious matters as claims of fraud or breach of fiduciary duty. In most cases, it will be reasonable for executors to take legal advice on remuneration and retain counsel for the passing of accounts. Since the estate owes it to the executors that they be properly remunerated, the executors, subject to just exceptions, should be fully indemnified for their costs incidental to realizing that right. 10 The Executors point out that the reasoning in Kanee was accepted by the Court in Re Wattersworth Estate 1995 CarswellOnt 2528 (Ont Ct J (Gen Div) at para. 38: Notwithstanding the authority of Widdifield on Executor's Accounts, I cannot accept as truly reflective of the law that the time spent by an estate solicitor responding to executor's questions concerning compensation allowed by law to them is not an allowable estate expense. [p.115-5th Edition (1967)] It is clearly in the estate's best interests that legitimate compensation be paid (certainly no more than what would be allowed in normal circumstances). I also happen to agree with the rationale followed by the presiding judge in [Kanee]… 11 It is not clear to me, however, that the approach in Kanee has been universally accepted. Both Kanee and Preboy have been cited in subsequent years, though largely without much analysis. 12 Moreover, as Mr. Anderson points out, Donald J. also stated in Kanee at para. 27 that “There will be cases where the executor's claim is outrageous or tainted by serious misconduct, and the discretion as to costs should be exercised differently.” Further, while the disagreement between Kanee and Preboy is noted, the following statement nevertheless appears in Carmen S. Theriault, ed., Widdifield on Executors and Trustees, 6th ed., loose-leaf (consulted on 3 July 2012) (Toronto: Thomson Canada Limited) ch. 4 at 4–21: Advice to an executor as to his right to compensation is for the personal benefit of the executor, and fees incurred to obtain the advice should not be charged against the estate. 13 Therefore, I do not think it can be said with certainty that executors are entitled to payment from the estate of legal fees incurred in respect of the determination of their appropriate compensation. Rather, I think the matter falls to be determined in accordance with the general rule that executors are entitled to be indemnified from the estate for expenses, including legal fees, reasonably and properly incurred by them in the course of their administration of that estate. I stress the words “reasonably and properly” because of the unique nature of the relationship between estate solicitors, executors and beneficiaries. In this respect, this comment from Preboy is apt: The solicitor is the solicitor for the executor, not the estate. Fees that he may charge the executor are only recoverable by the executor from the estate if it is shown that they are necessary and proper charges against the estate. 14 Similarly, the following statement appears in Widdifield at p. 4–8.3: Absent prior court approval or consent of all the beneficiaries, paying litigation accounts incurred in defending an action brought by one of the beneficiaries is not permitted. The law firm took the position that the estate was the client. The estate is not able to hire a lawyer. Until legal accounts are approved by either the court or the beneficiaries, the legal accounts are the sole responsibility of the estate trustee. The estate trustee had to reimburse the estate for the accounts that were paid, plus interest: Coppel v. Coppel Estate, [2001] O.J. No. 5246, 2001 CarswellOnt 4460 (Ont.S.C.J.) 15 It is clear, then, that executors are not entitled to assume that their legal fees will be reimbursed by the estate, regardless of circumstances or quantum. If an executor wishes to seek out “gold-plated” legal representation and/or to retain counsel to do work not necessarily required by the estate, he may do so, but he may expect to be indemnified only for the portion of that cost reasonably required for the administration of the estate. 21. Costs in Dependants Relief Act actions In Lafleur v. Lafleur, 2015 ABQB 644, Justice Greckol gave this summary of the law: 19 The Dependants Relief Act does not specify how costs should be awarded. Legislative guidance is provided by the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, rr 10.28–10.34. 20 The traditional English rule held that successful and unsuccessful parties to estate litigation could routinely recoup their costs from the estate on a substantial indemnity basis. However, appellate courts in Canada have questioned this traditional rule, suggesting there is insufficient principled reason to adhere to a special rule that conflicts directly with the conventional civil litigation costs rules. 21 Drawing from various authorities, Graesser J summarized the current principles of costs in estate litigation (Re Foote Estate, 2010 ABQB 197 at para 16, 484 AR 188): 1. The Court has a discretion with respect to costs, but that discretion must be exercised judicially; 2. The “modern” approach to costs in estate litigation requires careful scrutiny of the litigation to restrict unwarranted litigation and protect estates from being depleted by such litigation; 3. Payment of an unsuccessful party's costs out of the estate requires analysis of a number of factors: a. Did the testator cause the litigation? b. Was the challenge reasonable? c. Was the conduct of the parties reasonable? d. Was there an allegation of undue influence? e. Were there different issues or periods of time in which costs should differ? f. Were there offers to settle?; 4. There is a residual discretion where factors such as who initiated the proceedings, and the size of the estate may be relevant; 5. Costs for a successful claimant in family relief claims are generally awarded on a solicitor and client basis; 6. Costs in favour of an unsuccessful family relief claimant are an exception to the basic rule that costs follow the event; 7. Estate litigation is no longer treated as an exception to the basic rule that costs follow the event; 8. Costs will normally follow the event in estate litigation, unless the challenge to the estate was reasonable, or on the basis of a public policy exception recognizing society's interest in only probating valid wills. 22 This modern approach is a restatement of the conventional costs rule, with certain exceptions, including dependants relief litigation (St Onge Estate v Breau, 2009 NBCA 36 at para 62, 345 NBR (2d) 101 (“St Onge Estate”)). 23 Considering the sixth Foote point, one commentator stated that it is very seldom in dependants' relief litigation that courts decline to grant an unsuccessful applicant costs payable from the estate (Brian A Schnurr, Estate Litigation, vol 2, 2nd ed (Toronto: Carswell, 1994) (loose-leaf revision 5) at 19–19). This is because dependants' relief legislation is remedial, passed for social policy purposes. 24 As summarized in a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal, “[w]here the difficulties or ambiguities that give rise to the litigation are caused, in whole or in part, by the testator,” costs of all parties will be paid out of the estate (McDougald Estate v Gooderham (2005), 17 ETR (3d) 36 at para 78). Courts have characterized dependants' relief claims as those caused by the testator, and accordingly those where the unsuccessful litigant is more likely to obtain partial or full indemnification from the estate (Re Foote Estate at para 24; St Onge Estate at para 70). 25 Where costs are payable in dependants relief litigation, courts commonly order solicitor-client costs to all parties payable from the estate (Re Boje Estate, 2005 ABCA 73 at para 34, 363 AR 288; D (VT) (Next Friend of) v Spinelli Estate, 1998 ABQB 966, 229 AR 137; Stone (Public Trustee of) v Stone Estate (1994), 154 AR 307 (Alta QB)).

Evidence in Costs Applications In Mitran v.
Guarantee RV Centre Inc.
L.R.
(3d) 54 (Q.B.), counsel made submissions to the court as the “reasonableness” of certain costs being sought.
In the course of those submissions he made certain assertions of fact not found in the evidence.
In determining that those assertions by counsel could not be considered as evidence, Johnstone J. held, at p.

62, that “the evidence available on the costs application is restricted to sworn evidence” because “any submissions he made were merely hearsay.” 2. “Reasonableness” When considering the reasonableness or otherwise of an expenditure made by the defendant I must view the matter through the eyes of the defendant and in light of the problem facing it when the expenditure was made.
The test of reasonableness is not, in my opinion, entirely based on the importance of the expenditure to success at trial.
Hindsight may show that some liabilities assumed were, in the end, of little or no benefit.
The question is whether the expense was reasonable and proper in the light of the circumstances which existed at the time it was incurred.
The issues raised from time to time by the pleadings and by discovery and production are significant circumstances.
The magnitude of the expenditure in relation to the amount at risk in the proceedings is another important consideration.
In all cases the party taxing costs has the burden of showing that both the nature of the expense and its amount were reasonable and proper in the circumstances.
Petrogas Processing Ltd. v.
Westcoast Transmission Co.
384 (Q.B.), at 394, per O'Leary J.
Madam Justice Johnstone in MacCabe v.
Westlock Roman Catholic Separate School District No.
L.R.
(3d) 1 (Q.B.); additional reasons at (1999) 73 Alta.
L.R.
22–23, set forth the following factors to consider when assessing the reasonableness of a claimed disbursement: It is clear that an award for disbursements is within my discretion.
In determining whether or not a disbursement is reasonable, I may consider the following factors:
(a) the length of the trial
(b) its complexity
(c) the nature and number of the issues involved in the trial
(d) the degree of contest as to evidentiary matters
(e) the degree of contest as to credibility of witnesses, including professional expert witnesses
(f) the nature and number of the defenses mounted
(g) the requirement for and use of experts
(h) the use of models, tests and scientific evidence
(i) the nature and amount of damages at issue
(j) the relationship of the expeses claimed as costs to the amounts at issue in damages
(k) any agreement of counsel to share specific expense items.
Her Ladyship then quoted with approval O'Leary J.'s statement in Petrogas Processing Ltd. v.
Westcoast Transmission Co.
384 (Q.B.) (reproduced above).
She said that “the overriding consideration therefore is the reasonableness of the disbursement in light of the circumstances which existed at the time it was incurred” (p.
At p.
30 she relied on the following statement of Leggat J. in Morrissette v.
Smith (1990), 39 C.P.C.

S.C.): [the] Test was whether, at the time the expense was incurred, it was a proper disbursement in the sense of not being extravagant, negligent, mistaken or the result of excessive caution or excessive zeal, judged by the situation at the time when the expense was incurred.
Unnecessary litigation For a list of actions which have been found to constitute “unnecessary litigation”[Rule 10.33(2)d)], please see Condominium Corporation No 022 5899 v.
499430 Alberta Ltd, 2020 ABQB 233, 2020 CarswellAlta 625 at paragraphs 59–61.
Discretion with Respect to Costs In Chisholm v.

Lindsay, 2015 ABCA 179, the Court said: 44 As we see it, the purpose of the Rules of Court is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly, justly and expeditiously resolved either by a Court process in a timely and cost-effective way or in some other fashion, as the Rules contemplate.
In every case, the relevant inquiry will be whether there was a legitimate attempt to settle given the issues in dispute and mindful of the conduct of the litigation.
Such an approach encourages settlements without derogating from that referred to as the foundation of the formal Rules.

Maheasserts that notwithstanding strict compliance with the formal Rules of Court, a trial judge must be permitted to take account, in the context of other factors, of non-compliant offers made in good faith to settle litigation.
The first matter is to consider the Court's discretionary rights … the Court has a wide area of discretion in awarding costs under R.
601 of the Alberta Rules of Court.
See also s.
19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act, R.S.A.

Although the Court's discretion in ordering costs is traditionally very wide, it is not a discretion without bounds with the scope of such discretion being recently discussed by Mason J. in Pharand Ski Corp. v.
Alberta (1991), [81 Alta.
L.R.
398: While the court has a wide discretion when awarding costs, the discretion must be exercised judicially and in accordance with established principles.
This broad discretion comes from, and is based upon the absolute discretion vested in the Court of Chancery in England with respect to costs.

As such, it is to be exercised in accordance with the precepts and historical precedents established by that court and developed therefrom, by case law based upon a proper application and extension of those precedents.
See Andrews v.
Barnes (1887), 39 Ch.
D.
133 and Mobil Oil of Canada Limited v.
Canadian Superior Oil Limited and Neilsen, supra.
Claudio's Restaurant Group Inc. v.
Calgary (City) (1993), 15 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 141 (Q.B.), at 147–48, per Rooke J.
In Papaschase Indian Band No.
Canada (Attorney General) (2004), 45 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 72 (Q.B.), Slatter J. reviewed the discretion which may be exercised in matters of costs.
At p.
79, his Lordship said: The Court of Appeal in [Pauli v.
ACE INA Insurance (2005), 1 W.W.R.
12 (Alta.
C.A.)] recognized the usual rule that costs follow the event.

However, the Court held that this normal rule can be displaced when some or all of the following factors are present: (a) the decision resolves a new or unsettled point, and it was in the public interest that the point be settled.
In such cases it is relevant whether the litigants have a direct pecuniary interest in the proceedings, and whether the issue extends beyond the immediate interests of the parties.

While the Court recognized that all decisions have some precedential value, and that that did not mean that all litigation was in the public interest, it concluded that settling the point in the Pauli action was of public interest.
(b) Costs may not follow the event if a novel point is involved.
The Court held that the interpretation of the standard form of insurance contract at issue in Pauli raised a novel point.
(c) The Court also concluded that Pauli was a test case, which is another reason to depart from the normal costs rule.
While the class in Pauli was defined so widely that it would cover every person in Alberta with a similar claim, the Court held that the decision might prove persuasive in other similar actions.
(d) The Court noted that class actions were permitted in order to increase access to justice, and that exposing plaintiffs to costs would discourage meritorious class actions.

The Court noted that the representative plaintiffs could have expected to gain no more than $1,000.00 each if they had been successful, but they were now subject to a costs award of $115,000.00 to $125,000.00.
Bowes v.
Edmonton (City) (2005), 49 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 100 (Q.B.) is an interesting example of a court exercising its discretion regarding costs.
The Plaintiffs sued the City of Edmonton, alleging negligence and nuisance.
The City successfully defended the claims on the basis that the Plaintiffs had commenced their action beyond the limitation period, though the Court determined that the City had been negligent.
At pp.
101–102, Clackson J. made the following statements about the action: The City filed offers of judgment in September 2004 and withdrew those offers in December 2004.
The vast bulk of the time and expense which these cases consumed related to everything but limitation periods.
The usual rule is that costs follow the event.
However, the Plaintiffs argue that the Limitations Act resulted in an unjust and unfair deprivation of otherwise sound claims.
Therefore, the Plaintiffs argue that costs should be used as a means of ameliorating the inequity.
I agree that the Plaintiffs have been unfairly deprived.
That unfairness is however not attributable in any way to the City, it is inherent in limitations law and ultimate limitation periods.
There are instances where costs are awarded against a successful party.
However, that result usually occurs where the successful party has been guilty of some misconduct that warrants censure.
The City is guilty of no misconduct in this case.
The inequity here is statutory in origin.

Therefore, there is no good reason why the usual rule should be departed from in this case. … Having found that the Defendant was guilty of no misconduct, having found any “unfairness” in result was a consequence of the nature of limitation date statutes, and having found “no good reason” to depart from the usual rule, Clackson J. then said (at p.
102): … However, it is appropriate in my view to analyze the result more particularly than simply who won and who lost.
As I have said, this trial was dominated by issues of negligence and nuisance.
The vast bulk of the evidence and effort was directed at the issue of negligence.
The Plaintiffs were successful in that regard.
The matter of the Plaintiffs' nuisance claims were based in large measure upon the evidence and arguments relating to the negligence claims.
The City successfully defended itself on the nuisance claims.
In my view, a costs award should reflect all of those results and the history of the action to the date of trial.
As well the costs award should reflect the fact that the Plaintiffs did not achieve a result that “beat” the offer made by the City prior to trial.
Finally, the costs award should reflect the relative expenditure of time and effort on the individual issues which were in dispute.
Having regard to all of those factors, I award one set of costs on Column 5 of Schedule C of the Rules of Court to the Plaintiffs for all steps taken up to December 2, 2004.
Thereafter I award the Plaintiffs 70% of one set of costs on Column 5 through to and including the trial and the determination of costs.
The Plaintiffs' proper disbursements are awarded to them in full.
I award the City 30% of one set of double costs on Column 5 from December 2, 2004 through the trial and the determination of costs.
The City's proper disbursements are awarded to them in full.
Both sides are entitled to include second counsel fee in their Bills of Costs.

The unusual end result is that the successful Defendant, who properly relied on the limitation statute enacted by the Legislature, was guilty of no misconduct in the action, and had made a formal offer of settlement which was not accepted by the Plaintiff, was ordered to pay to the unsuccessful Plaintiffs costs up to the date of the withdrawal of the defence settlement offer, and was itself only awarded 30% of its double costs after the date of the withdrawal.

The rationale for the decision seems to have been that the majority of the trial was directed at the issue of negligence which the Plaintiffs established but the Defendant avoided the consequences of that finding because the limitation statute gave the defendant immunity.

However, the decision does effectively penalize the Defendant for simply relying on legislation (Limitations Act) the provisions of which the Legislature passed having determined what was a proper balance between those seeking redress for wrongs and those who must defend themselves against claims.
In Lee v.
Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board) (2005), 386 A.R.
86 (Q.B.), Hillier J. said, at p.

101: The Court may exercise its discretion to deny costs where there is (1) misconduct either before or after the lawsuit, (2) miscarriage in the procedure or (3) oppressive and vexatious conduct of proceedings….
In 1022049 Alberta Ltd. v.
Medicine Hat (City), 2006 ABQB 208, 2006 CarswellAlta 749, 400 A.R.
(6th) 342, Erb J. considered whether the Court should consider post-judgment evidence when determining costs.
At p.
250, her Ladyship said: 15 Post hearing evidence relating to the merits or conduct of a party should not be considered unless there is clear connection between that evidence and the proceedings.
For example, post hearing evidence of fraudulent conduct such as deliberately misleading the court could be considered in determining costs regardless of which party was successful at trial.
16 The rules of evidence apply to a costs hearing.
The Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook at p.
576 notes that “inadmissible material cannot be looked at by the court, even when considering costs.” In Anderson v.
Amoco Canada Oil & Gas, [2002] A.J.
No.

A failure to comply with the Rules will generally not be fatal so long as any prejudice to the other side can be remedied by an award of costs, an adjournment, or some other type of relief.
This general rule has many manifestations, but some of the more specific ones are: (a) a missed deadline in the Rules will not be fatal if any prejudice can be remedied by costs.
(b) if a judgment is entered or a step is taken in default of appearance of one of the parties, the step taken in default can often be opened up.
(c) if a pleading is for some reason deficient or inadequate, an amendment will generally be allowed, so long as there is no prejudice that cannot be remedied.
(d) late applications for adjournments of scheduled court appearances will often be granted, again so long as any prejudice can be remedied in some way.
This prejudice-based system of proceedings has been criticized on the basis that it is too unstructured, and it leads to delay and added expense.
Nevertheless, it remains the general rule governing civil practice in Alberta.
Apart from the general principle that procedural missteps that can be remedied will not be fatal, there are some specific rules relating to particular types of missteps.
Without attempting to state in detail the law or the tests applicable, some examples include:
(a) there are some specific Rules, such as Rules 190 and 538(4), which deal with the consequences of missing specific time requirements in the Rules.

(b) in opening up a noting in default, the moving party must generally provide some explanation for non-appearance, must show that the application to open up was brought promptly, and must demonstrate a triable defence.
(c) as a general rule, Rule 141 provides that an amending party is not entitled to costs of the amendment of a pleading.
(This Rule is perhaps somewhat academic given the repeal of the specific item in Schedule “C” that used to allow a separate fee for amendment of pleadings.)
(d) where a late adjournment is granted, costs will often be awarded for wasted preparation, keeping in mind that not all preparation will be completely lost.
In any of these situations, “thrown away costs” may be awarded as a method of negating any prejudice that might otherwise fall on the responding party.

What costs are “thrown away” will depend on the particular type of application being brought, and the cases must be examined to see the particular context in which they were decided.8 In dealing with what are truly “thrown away costs”, all of these procedural situations break down into two parts:

(a) there is initially some procedural misstep by the applicant party, be that the faulty drafting of a pleading, the failure to attend in court on the appropriate date, the failure to be ready to proceed on a scheduled trial date, or the missing of a deadline.

This procedural misstep causes the responding party to take some step (such as getting a default judgment, preparing for a trial that is adjourned, or responding to the faulty pleading), or perhaps it may simply cause delay and require an application to comply with the Rules (in the case of a missed deadline).
When the applicant later tries to correct its misstep, the action taken by the respondent becomes “wasted” or “thrown away”.
(b) the second step is then to resolve whether the applicant who made the misstep is entitled to some relief.

At this stage of the proceedings, the applicant who committed the procedural misstep alleges that he or she is within the general rule that missteps are allowed so long as there is no prejudice that is not remediable in some way.
The respondent might concede that the applicant has met the test, or may assert that the applicant is not entitled to relief, and resist the application.
There may then be a contested proceeding over whether the applicant is entitled to relief. … Thrown Away Costs There is conflicting case law on the concept of thrown away costs.
There are two competing philosophies.

The first is that the applicant who made the misstep is seeking an indulgence, and must pay all the costs of seeking the indulgence, even if it is clear on the authorities that the applicant is entitled to the indulgence: Fox v.
Bourget (1987), 17 C.P.C.
Dist.
Ct.) citing Aliferis v.
Parfeniuk (1985), 1 C.P.C.
C.A.), although Aliferis does not appear to state any general principle to that effect.

On the one hand, if the applicant asserts a right to fix an error, and wins in the face of resistence to that relief, the applicant should get costs.

On the other hand, it is asserted that the party who made the error should pay, because it caused the problem and is seeking an indulgence. … The Court of Queen's Bench Costs Manual, prepared by the Taxing Officers, defines “thrown away costs” as follows: “Thrown Away Costs” Are those that a party would not have incurred save for the actions of another party.
