Consider the following: Item # Description Thrown Away Cost?

1 Pleadings (drafting, filing & serving Statement of Claim) no 6(2) Ex Parte Application for a Substitutional Service Order no 1 Noting in Default (a component of Item 1—get a proportion yes of the Item) 2 Uncontested Assessment Application yes 5 Examination on Affidavit re: application to set aside default yes judgment 7(1) Defence of Application to Set Aside Default Judgment yes The Manual treats as thrown away not only the wasted effort of the respondent, but also the steps taken by the applicant to determine if it has a right to correct the original error.18 The general pattern in these cases is that when a party makes a procedural misstep, that party will then assert to the respondent that it has the right to correct that misstep if it eliminates all the prejudice.
For example, it may assert that it has the right to amend a defective pleading, on payment of the costs of any wasted effort by the respondent.
It might assert a right to open up a noting in default, because it has met the legal test for doing that (supra, para.

The respondent can do one of two things: it can acknowledge that the applicant has the right to fix the misstep, because the applicable test has been met, including that any prejudice can be eliminated on appropriate terms, or it can deny that the applicant has the right to correct the misstep.
In the latter situation, a new sub-dispute is created.

When this issue is litigated, the general rule should be that costs follow the event, subject of course to the Court's general jurisdiction over costs.
Granting costs to an unsuccessful party only encourages unreasonable opposition to relief to which the applicant is entitled.

Therefore, as a general rule where (for example) one party asserts a right to amend pleadings, and the other party denies that right, and the amending party must take the matter to court, costs should follow the event.
If the applicant succeeds in its motion to amend, it should get costs.
Rule 141 says simply that the amending party must bear the costs of the amendment (as I have previously mentioned, supra, para.
7(c), a reference to a now repealed part of Schedule “C”).
Rule 141 does not say that the applicant must pay the costs of the fight over whether it has the right to amend, even if it wins that fight.
That would be a most undesirable result, because it would mean that the respondents on motions like that could defend them with impunity, knowing that win or lose they would receive costs.
Absent some positive misconduct, the successful moving party should get costs of the motion to permit the amendment.
Likewise, if a party is noted in default, but asserts that it has met the test for opening up a default, it should be entitled to costs if successful.
If the respondent denies that the defaulting party has the right to open up the default, and forces the matter to Chambers, then costs should follow the event.
Again, it would be an undesirable result to allow respondents to defend such applications regardless of the merits of the applicant's position.
The applicant may have caused the noting in default, but it did not cause the subsequent court battle about whether it was entitled to open up the noting in default.
With applications to adjourn, a distinction should be drawn between the effort that will be wasted if there is an adjournment, and the dispute over the right to an adjournment.

In principle, if the applicant asserts a right to adjournment, and under the prevailing rules and practice the applicant is entitled to that adjournment, then if the respondent resists, costs should follow the event.
However, if the adjournment is the result of some fault of the applicant, the applicant is often required to pay the costs of the adjournment application, even if successful.
This is an exception to Rule 607.
It should be noted that in these situations the costs of determining whether the applicant is entitled to be relieved of its procedural misstep is not really “wasted”.
There is a dispute over the rights of the applicant to relief from its error, and the application resolves that dispute.
Those efforts are not “wasted”, because the dispute must be resolved.

Furthermore, those proceedings are not a direct result of the procedural misstep of the applicant; they are really brought on by the respondent's failure to accept that the applicant has made out its right to be relieved of the consequence of its procedural misstep.
Where the applicant is entitled to relief the respondent should not unreasonably litigate the point.
As a result, the rule that costs go to the successful party (Rule 607) should prevail over any rule about “wasted” costs.
In summary, a distinction should be drawn between:
(a) the costs of the wasted work caused by the procedural misstep that is the source of the problem, and
(b) litigating the dispute over whether the person who took the misstep has the right to fix it.

The principle that the Rules are prejudice-based, and that procedural errors should be forgiven if prejudice can be eliminated, must be balanced against the other rule that costs generally go to the successful party: Rule 607.
Subject to the overriding discretion of the judge over costs, only the first category of costs (paragraph (a)) are “thrown away”.

Purpose of Costs I am aware that the principle and purpose behind the wording of party-and-party costs is to provide indemnity to the person entitled to them Such Rules of Court are not designed for the purpose of punishing, penalizing or benefitting a party to an action.

In Alberta, except in unique circumstances, party-and-party costs will not approach indemnification of the successful party and thus it is more accurate to describe the awarding of costs as a contribution toward the successful party's expense in prosecuting or defending the action.
Wenden v.
Trikha (1992), 1 Alta L.R.
(3d) 283 (Q.B.), at 293, per Murray J.
And McDonald J. said: While the allocation of costs of a lawsuit is always in the discretion of the court, the exercise of that discretion must be consistent with established principles and practice.
It is traditionally accepted in Canada's common law provinces that as a general rule the successful party recovers its costs from the unsuccessful party.
However, such recovery is normally on a party-and-party basis.
That is, the costs recoverable are those fees fixed for the steps in the proceeding by a schedule of fees (Sched.
C. in Alberta's Rules of Court), plus reasonable disbursements.
It is not intended that the successful party receive full indemnification of those fees and disbursements which it would be charged by its counsel.
In England the degree of indemnification appears to be considerably higher than is normal in Canada.
In almost all jurisdictions of the United States of America the rule is that no costs are recoverable by the successful party.
The Canadian practice reflects an attempt to balance two conflicting interests.

On the one hand, it is argued that if a party is successful and there are no circumstances constituting blameworthiness in the conduct of the litigation by that party, it is unfair to require the successful party to bear any costs incurred by his counsel in prosecuting or defending the action.

On the other hand, it is argued that if the unsuccessful party is required to bear all the costs of the successful party, citizens will be unduly hesitant to sue to assert their rights (even valid ones) or to defend their rights when sued.
The partial indemnity practice as it exists in Canada is a compromise intended to give some scope in practice for each of the conflicting policy considerations.
When the case is of considerable magnitude and complexity, the practice in Alberta contemplates that the court may order the unsuccessful party to pay a multiple of the fees that are fixed by Sched.
C.
But even then it is not intended that there be full indemnity, except in extraordinary circumstances.
Reese v.
Alberta (1993), 5 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 40 (Q.B.), at 44–45, per McDonald J.
Consider Complexity and Difficulty of Proceedings In addition to s.
19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act and the relevant Rules of Court, McCarthy v.
Bd. of Trustees, supra, is authority for the proposition that the difficulty and complexity of the proceedings are relevant in considering the scale of party-party costs to be awarded.
Similarly, in the Alberta Court of Appeal case of Calbar Securities Ltd. v.
Toole Peet Co.
L.R.
(2d) 286 … which upheld the trial judge's award of costs on triple col.
5 with no limiting rule to apply, the late McGillivray C.J.A. held at pp.

287–88: The court is of the opinion that the scale of costs and the exclusion of the limiting rule cannot be based on the number of parties who are to pay the costs, but should depend upon the amount involved, the complexity and importance of the issues, and the length of trial.
In New Brunswick, the Court of Appeal in Williams v.
New Brunswick; St.
John v.
Williams; Chubb Indust.
Ltd. v.
St.

299 at 320 … held that, although the amount recovered in a lawsuit has always been important, it … is not the sole criterion and in fixing costs the Court may consider other matters including the complexity of the proceedings, the importance of the issues, the conduct of the parties, the manner in which the proceedings were conducted and any other matter relevant to the question of costs.
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v.
Canadian Commercial Bank (1987), 50 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 1 (Q.B.), at 10–11, per Wachowich J.
When punitive damages have been awarded In Indutech Canada Ltd. v.
Gibbs Pipe Distributors Ltd., 2012 ABQB 425, 2012 CarswellAlta 1909, 84 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 55, the successful Plaintiffs sought enhanced costs.
The defendants submitted that since punitive damages had been awarded against them, costs should not be enhanced.

Madam Justice Romaine disagreed, and, at paragraphs 11–12, said: 11 The Gibbs Group Defendants submit that where a party has been punished for misconduct by an award of punitive damages, as was the case here, courts have been disinclined to punish that party further through a costs award: 539618 Ontario Ltd. v.
Stathopoulos (1989), 17 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 159 (Ont.H.C.J.) at para.

12 It may be more accurate to say that an award of punitive damages may be a factor in considering enhanced costs, since the rules and case authority in Alberta do not preclude the consideration of misconduct at the costs stage of proceedings, whether or not punitive damages have been found to be appropriate.
Punitive damages reflect the misconduct of the Gibbs Group Defendants over the course of the Agency Agreement.

An enhanced costs award reflects misconduct during the course of the litigation, and there is evidence of such misconduct in the findings of credibility made with respect to various of the Gibbs Group Defendants.
Justice Romaine's decision was unsuccessfully appealed (Indutech Canada Ltd. v.
Gibbs Pipe Distributors Ltd., 2013 ABCA 111, 2013 CarswellAlta 957, 544 A.R.
L.R.

The Court said, at paragraphs 100, and 102–106: 100 In a companion appeal, the appellants appeal the trial judge's awarded enhanced costs under some categories available under Column 5 of Schedule C of the Rules of Court.
They do not contest the award of enhanced costs in relation to other categories.

Her award elevated the costs payable by the appellants above the $285,000 which would have otherwise been ordered paid by them. … 102 She rejected the argument that enhanced costs should not be awarded because the harm they addressed was met by the award of punitive damages.
Her award was grounded in the nature of the litigation itself.

She accepted that an award of punitive damages should reflect misconduct prior to the commencement of the litigation and of enhanced costs misconduct during the course of the litigation; see Polar Ice Express Inc v Arctic Glacier Inc, 2009 ABCA 20 at paras 21–22, 446 AR 295.

She found such misconduct “in the findings of credibility” made with respect to various of the [appellants], notwithstanding that she then proceeded to give specific reasons for each enhancement which did not rest on this finding of misconduct.
103 No authority precludes an award of enhanced costs because punitive damages were also awarded in the proper case.
Judges have, in some cases, declined to make such an award upon concluding that remedies given, including punitive damages, were sufficient to account for the wrongdoing of the unsuccessful party.
The trial judge implicitly concluded otherwise, from her comments relating to her findings of litigation misconduct.
104 Similarly, while some judges have declined to find litigation misconduct simply because of credibility findings made against certain witnesses, no authority precludes the award for that reason.

In any event, the nature and depth of the negative credibility findings made against the appellants' witnesses elevates this case from the more typical situation where a trial judge simply accepts the evidence of one witness over that of others.
For example, the appellants produced 11 separate affidavits of records.

There was evidence that preparation for questioning took an inordinate amount of time because the transgressions could be uncovered only through detailed examination of these records, encompassing between 15,000 to 20,000 pages of documents produced by the appellants.
105 The enhanced costs award would have been justified here simply on the basis of the complexity and duration of the ligation, without reference to litigation misconduct.

That practice is often followed by a judge electing to give a multiple of the appropriate column in Schedule C to reflect atypical or extraordinary aspects in the procedure leading up to judgment in a given matter.
This consideration more than offsets any concern of double-compensation arising from the award of punitive damages for pre-litigation conduct.
106 The trial judge's award of enhanced costs lay well within her properly exercised discretion; see Court of Queen's Bench Act, RSA 2000, c C-31, s 21.

Adjournments I assume that when the bar decided to adopt the amounts set out in item 25 of the tariff, it had in mind that these are the costs that would be awarded, except in exceptional circumstances… … It is only where the parties make out a special case for additional costs that an amount other than the tariff amount should be awarded.
It may well be appropriate to take into account “fault”in relation to the need for an adjournment in determining if something other than the tariff item should be applied.
For example, if the party whose action necessitated the adjournment was somehow “at fault”, it may be entirely appropriate to award thrown away costs, or even punitive costs.
However, where there is no “fault”, and there are no exceptional circumstances the tariff should apply.
Lines v.
Brink (1994), 24 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 227 (Q.B.), at 238–39, per Veit J.
Compassion is Not a Factor In P.
MacDonald (1999), 242 A.R.
134 (Q.B.), an unsuccessful plaintiff sought relief from the provisions of R 605(5).
At p.
142, Veit J. said: The plaintiff asks for the court's compassion.
However, the adoption of the plaintiff's argument would result in a deprivation perpetrated on the defendants.
It is inappropriate, therefore, to say that compassion is an appropriate factor.
It seems to me, rather, that fairness and equity are the benchmarks here.
By those standards, it is fair to apply the provisions of rule 605(5) which provisions were known to the plaintiff before she opened the trial.
Costs in Estate Litigation In Chabros v.
Anderson, 2012 ABQB 517, 2012 CarswellAlta 1422, 79 E.T.R.
(3d) 317, Justice Clark considered Rules 10.33(1) and (2).
He said, at paragraphs 6–15: 6 These are the rules which govern in, for lack of better term, “ordinary” civil litigation.
However, both parties pointed out that costs are treated differently in estate litigation.
The Executors referred to the “historical” and “modern” approaches to costs in estate litigation.
7 Historically, it was common practice in estate matters for courts to award costs of all parties out of the estate.
This approach, however, has been out of favour for several years.
As noted by Graesser J. of this Court in Re Foote Estate, 2010 ABQB 197 at para.

16, the “modern” approach to costs in estate litigation “requires careful scrutiny of the litigation to restrict unwarranted litigation and protect estates from being depleted by such litigation.” In more recent years, the courts have recognized that awards of costs operate to the detriment of estate beneficiaries.
See, inter alia, Babchuk v.
Kutz, 2007 ABQB 88 and my own reasons in Johnson v.
Beers, 1999 ABQB 723, 252 AR 187.
Thus, the general approach now in estate litigation is that costs follow the event unless the challenge to the will was reasonable or an exception can be justified on public policy grounds.
8 Of course, this case did not concern a challenge to the validity of the Will or proceedings to determine its proper construction.

Rather, the points at issue are the proper compensation payable to the Executors for their administration of the Estate and, as a related matter, the Executors' right to be indemnified for expenses reasonably and properly incurred in the course of administration.
The Executors rely upon this statement from Jennifer J.
Jenkins, Compensation & Duties of Estate Trustees, Guardians & Attorneys (Toronto: Canada Law Book, 2011) at para.
22:20.20: It should be appreciated that any discussion contrasting the traditional approach to costs with the developing mindset is too simple an analysis.
The issue of costs has its own particular slant, depending on the type of litigation, which hinges primarily on the role of the estate trustee.
For example, a contested passing of accounts is considered to be a significant part of the administration of an estate.

Thus an estate trustee is entitled to take an adversarial position in defence of his or her administration and claim for compensation and, generally speaking, the starting point is that the estate trustee and the beneficiaries are awarded costs as a legitimate expense of the estate.
9 The Executors also referred to the following comments from Donald J.
(as he then was) in Re Kanee Estate (1991) 41 ETR 263 (BCSC) at paras.
17, 23, 24 and 26: There is much force in the argument advanced by Mr.

Wilson that when remuneration is the only issue, the executors are acting in their own self-interest and not for the benefit of the estate and, therefore, they and any contending parties should be treated as ordinary litigants as far as costs are concerned.
He endeavours to support this proposition by a decision of the Saskatchewan Surrogate Court in Re Preboy Estate (1989), 72 Sask.
R.
33 (Surr.
Ct.), aff'd (1989), 74 Sask.
R.
223 (C.A.), where at p.
43 [72 Sask.

R.] McLellan J. said: There can be no justification for the solicitors charging the beneficiaries a fee to research the law to find out what they and the executors are entitled to charge the estate. … The litigation model does not, in my opinion, fit the circumstances of this case.
Executors do not step outside the estate to deal with the question of remuneration; the subject is customarily dealt with as part of the passing-of-accounts process.
This is so because of the intimate connection it has with the estate.
I cannot agree with Re Preboy, supra, if it purports to lay down a statement of general principle.
The Court in that case did not elaborate any reasons for the statement quoted above.

It is inapplicable to the case at Bar because, as the Master rightly held, it is inappropriate to set up an adversity in interest between the estate and the executors in the settlement of remuneration.
Subject to considerations of reasonableness and honesty, the question of costs should be dealt with in the same way for remuneration as for the other aspects in the passing of accounts.

Executors are entitled to be paid for their work. … The questioning of remuneration should not be considered in any way analogous to such truly litigious matters as claims of fraud or breach of fiduciary duty.
In most cases, it will be reasonable for executors to take legal advice on remuneration and retain counsel for the passing of accounts.
Since the estate owes it to the executors that they be properly remunerated, the executors, subject to just exceptions, should be fully indemnified for their costs incidental to realizing that right.
10 The Executors point out that the reasoning in Kanee was accepted by the Court in Re Wattersworth Estate 1995 CarswellOnt 2528 (Ont Ct J (Gen Div) at para.

38: Notwithstanding the authority of Widdifield on Executor's Accounts, I cannot accept as truly reflective of the law that the time spent by an estate solicitor responding to executor's questions concerning compensation allowed by law to them is not an allowable estate expense.
[p.115-5th Edition (1967)] It is clearly in the estate's best interests that legitimate compensation be paid (certainly no more than what would be allowed in normal circumstances).
I also happen to agree with the rationale followed by the presiding judge in [Kanee]… 11 It is not clear to me, however, that the approach in Kanee has been universally accepted.
Both Kanee and Preboy have been cited in subsequent years, though largely without much analysis.
12 Moreover, as Mr.
Anderson points out, Donald J. also stated in Kanee at para.

27 that “There will be cases where the executor's claim is outrageous or tainted by serious misconduct, and the discretion as to costs should be exercised differently.” Further, while the disagreement between Kanee and Preboy is noted, the following statement nevertheless appears in Carmen S.
Theriault, ed., Widdifield on Executors and Trustees, 6th ed., loose-leaf (consulted on 3 July 2012) (Toronto: Thomson Canada Limited) ch.
4 at 4–21: Advice to an executor as to his right to compensation is for the personal benefit of the executor, and fees incurred to obtain the advice should not be charged against the estate.

13 Therefore, I do not think it can be said with certainty that executors are entitled to payment from the estate of legal fees incurred in respect of the determination of their appropriate compensation.

Rather, I think the matter falls to be determined in accordance with the general rule that executors are entitled to be indemnified from the estate for expenses, including legal fees, reasonably and properly incurred by them in the course of their administration of that estate.
I stress the words “reasonably and properly” because of the unique nature of the relationship between estate solicitors, executors and beneficiaries.
In this respect, this comment from Preboy is apt: The solicitor is the solicitor for the executor, not the estate.
Fees that he may charge the executor are only recoverable by the executor from the estate if it is shown that they are necessary and proper charges against the estate.
14 Similarly, the following statement appears in Widdifield at p.
4–8.3: Absent prior court approval or consent of all the beneficiaries, paying litigation accounts incurred in defending an action brought by one of the beneficiaries is not permitted.
The law firm took the position that the estate was the client.
The estate is not able to hire a lawyer.
Until legal accounts are approved by either the court or the beneficiaries, the legal accounts are the sole responsibility of the estate trustee.
The estate trustee had to reimburse the estate for the accounts that were paid, plus interest: Coppel v.
Coppel Estate, [2001] O.J.
No.

5246, 2001 CarswellOnt 4460 (Ont.S.C.J.) 15 It is clear, then, that executors are not entitled to assume that their legal fees will be reimbursed by the estate, regardless of circumstances or quantum.

If an executor wishes to seek out “gold-plated” legal representation and/or to retain counsel to do work not necessarily required by the estate, he may do so, but he may expect to be indemnified only for the portion of that cost reasonably required for the administration of the estate.
Costs in Dependants Relief Act actions In Lafleur v.
Lafleur, 2015 ABQB 644, Justice Greckol gave this summary of the law: 19 The Dependants Relief Act does not specify how costs should be awarded.
Legislative guidance is provided by the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, rr 10.28–10.34.
20 The traditional English rule held that successful and unsuccessful parties to estate litigation could routinely recoup their costs from the estate on a substantial indemnity basis.

However, appellate courts in Canada have questioned this traditional rule, suggesting there is insufficient principled reason to adhere to a special rule that conflicts directly with the conventional civil litigation costs rules.
21 Drawing from various authorities, Graesser J summarized the current principles of costs in estate litigation (Re Foote Estate, 2010 ABQB 197 at para 16, 484 AR 188): 1.
The Court has a discretion with respect to costs, but that discretion must be exercised judicially; 2.
The “modern” approach to costs in estate litigation requires careful scrutiny of the litigation to restrict unwarranted litigation and protect estates from being depleted by such litigation; 3.
Payment of an unsuccessful party's costs out of the estate requires analysis of a number of factors: a.
Did the testator cause the litigation? b.
Was the challenge reasonable? c.
Was the conduct of the parties reasonable? d.
Was there an allegation of undue influence? e.
Were there different issues or periods of time in which costs should differ? f.
Were there offers to settle?; 4.
There is a residual discretion where factors such as who initiated the proceedings, and the size of the estate may be relevant; 5.
Costs for a successful claimant in family relief claims are generally awarded on a solicitor and client basis; 6.
Costs in favour of an unsuccessful family relief claimant are an exception to the basic rule that costs follow the event; 7.
Estate litigation is no longer treated as an exception to the basic rule that costs follow the event; 8.

Costs will normally follow the event in estate litigation, unless the challenge to the estate was reasonable, or on the basis of a public policy exception recognizing society's interest in only probating valid wills.

22 This modern approach is a restatement of the conventional costs rule, with certain exceptions, including dependants relief litigation (St Onge Estate v Breau, 2009 NBCA 36 at para 62, 345 NBR (2d) 101 (“St Onge Estate”)).

23 Considering the sixth Foote point, one commentator stated that it is very seldom in dependants' relief litigation that courts decline to grant an unsuccessful applicant costs payable from the estate (Brian A Schnurr, Estate Litigation, vol 2, 2nd ed (Toronto: Carswell, 1994) (loose-leaf revision 5) at 19–19).
This is because dependants' relief legislation is remedial, passed for social policy purposes.

24 As summarized in a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal, “[w]here the difficulties or ambiguities that give rise to the litigation are caused, in whole or in part, by the testator,” costs of all parties will be paid out of the estate (McDougald Estate v Gooderham
(3d) 36 at para 78).

Courts have characterized dependants' relief claims as those caused by the testator, and accordingly those where the unsuccessful litigant is more likely to obtain partial or full indemnification from the estate (Re Foote Estate at para 24
St Onge Estate at para 70).
25 Where costs are payable in dependants relief litigation, courts commonly order solicitor-client costs to all parties payable from the estate (Re Boje Estate, 2005 ABCA 73 at para 34, 363 AR 288
D (VT) (Next Friend of) v Spinelli Estate, 1998 ABQB 966, 229 AR 137
Stone (Public Trustee of) v Stone Estate
